en.html:
Railway travel and I had met very seldom.

Where I grew up was proper back-country. No station, no tracks. After conscription I did travel by train on military service, but only a few times even then.
Demobilized, back home, employed: another two or three.

Had Rokuhara not restricted civilian rail travel after taking power, perhaps I would have made a few more journeys. ...Though in the company, not one person rated me suitable for outside work. Traveling for my own pleasure was also not my habit. So the number was hardly waiting to become magnificent.

One hand could count my railway experience. The speed, the inside of the carriage, the landscape running past the window—I was still not used to any of it. Everything retained the freshness of a new acquaintance.

過去、鉄道を利用する機会は少なかった。

　育った土地は文字通りの片田舎で駅も線路もなく、
長じて徴兵を受け軍役に就いた折には汽車に乗ること
もあったが、それとてせいぜい数度ばかり。
　復員して郷里に戻り、就職してからほんの二、三度。

　六波羅が政権掌握後に民間人の鉄道利用を規制して
いなければ、もう少し回数は増えていたろう。
　……会社では俺を外勤向きと評価する人などおらず、
<ruby>私<rt>し</rt></ruby>で旅行する趣味もなかったから、高は知れているが。

　そんな次第で、俺は片手で数えて足りる程度にしか
鉄道の旅の経験がない。
　この速さも、内装も、窓の外を流れる風景も、まだ
慣れず、斬新な印象の残るものだった。

en.html:
Sayo"Not quite settled, are we?"
Kageaki"A little unsettled, yes. It is embarrassing."
Sayo"Bear with it a little, sir."
Kageaki"No, no, I am not uncomfortable. Do not trouble yourself over that. ...You, madam, appear entirely at ease."
Sayo"Each wrinkle is one experience accounted for. When madam and I were living in Europe, especially, trains were an everyday affair."
Kageaki"I hear electric trains are common there now."
Sayo"Indeed. On the short city routes, they are probably the main kind already. Between cities, steam locomotives are still very much in the majority..."
Sayo"Though some places appear to be using electric locomotives as well."
Kageaki"? Is that a different thing from an electric train?"
Sayo"What you mean, Minato sir, is the arrangement where the individual carriages have their own power. In the other arrangement, an electric locomotive pulls the carriages behind it."
Kageaki"Ah... understood. So the ordinary steam locomotive, only made electric."
Sayo"Correct. But Minato sir, do not release that observation into the world so carelessly. Let certain railway fanatics hear you, and bas. You have booked yourself a lecture."
Sayo"Forty-two hours, by my estimate. First, how both systems came into being. Then the machinery in full detail, every tiny difference, their actual operation, and finally their future prospects. Nothing will be left unexplained. You least of all will be left alone."
Kageaki"? ...I see."

さよ「左様でございますね。市街地の短距離路線 では既にそちらが主流でしょうか。 　都市間鉄道はまだまだ蒸気機関車が多数を 占めておりますが……」

en.html:
What this warning was about, I could not say.

The window’s moving picture was gradually leaving peaceful farmland for deep mountain country. Every so often, a bridge carried us over a river.

Sunlight struck the water and came flashing back. A child would perhaps have made a great excitement of it.
In that almost empty carriage, this was what I found myself thinking.

Kageaki"...Still. Getting aboard was surprisingly simple."
Sayo"The trains leaving Aizu are reportedly packed with rich people wishing to escape before the war. A civilian going in the opposite direction, toward the center of Aizu, must have very special tastes indeed."
Sayo"Seats? Take whichever you like. Provided you can pay the fare, which compared with Europe is a joke too expensive to laugh at."
Kageaki"Yes. But that is not the matter I had in mind. Aizu is practically under martial law now—"
Kageaki"I expected every train to be requisitioned by the army. Or, if some room remained for civilians, at least a strict examination before we were allowed aboard."

Kageaki"And once aboard, this becomes the fastest and most efficient way..."
Sayo"Sit and wait. The arriving happens for you. Perhaps our only concern is that if trouble starts inside, getting out becomes difficult."
Kageaki"There is a possibility of that?"
Sayo"To call it impossible would be overconfidence. A company of the Sasagawa army is traveling with us. In another carriage."
Kageaki"...Meeting them face to face could become somewhat troublesome."
Sayo"It could, yes. ...But these are reservists called back into service."
Sayo"Apparently their work is logistics. Their spirits and equipment seem no grander than that requires. Carelessness, no. Great anxiety, also not necessary."

The old chamberlain gave her ho-ho laugh. I nodded, then closed my mouth.

Without noticing the turn, I found my eyes on the woman who had not spoken once since we boarded.

en.html:
Captain Ootori was watching the scenery.
No. That was my careless first conclusion.

Somewhere else her mind had gone. Her eyes faced the view, but stayed at one angle. The changing landscape hardly drew a response.

Not outside, then. Was she looking within? What was there for those narrow eyes to see?
What feeling inside this woman, Kanae Ootori—

Such prying was not usual business for me. Perhaps the sight of her lost in thought had drawn me in.

Unlike the Captain I normally knew, now she seemed a woman in the ordinary sense. Why, I could not say.
Fragile, uncertain. Delicate, almost faint.

Like when I had seen her playing the double bass.
Like that, yes, but not the same. Then she had a clear intention. It led the notes and made music of them. Now, something of that purpose was missing from her face.

A child who had lost the road home.

Alone in a strange place. Nothing there to turn to.

大鳥大尉は風景を眺めている。
　否――正確には違う。

　心ここに在らぬ<ruby>態<rt>てい</rt></ruby>だった。
　眼差しは景色に向けられてはいるものの、その角度
は固定されて動かず、地形の移り変わりにも<ruby>殆<rt>ほとん</rt></ruby>ど反応
しない。

　外ではなく内面を見ているのか。
　彼女の細い双眸は、今。だとすると、そこには何が
映っているのだろう。

　大鳥香奈枝という女性の、如何なる心情が――

　柄にもなくそんな詮索めいた欲求を起こしたのは、
沈思する彼女に心を惹かれたからかもしれない。

　普段の大尉と異なり、どうしてか、今の彼女は通俗
的な意味において女性と見えた。
　儚く、危うい。<ruby>繊<rt>そび</rt></ruby>やかで、淡い。

　<ruby>嘗<rt>かつ</rt></ruby>て見た、<ruby>弦楽器<rt>コントラバス</rt></ruby>を奏でる彼女に似ている。

な意思があり、それが音色を導き<ruby>楽<rt>がく</rt></ruby>に仕上げていた。
しかし今、彼女の<ruby>貌<rt>かお</rt></ruby>はその意思をどこか、欠いている。

　家路を見失った迷い子のようでもあった。

　寄る辺ない異境にただ独り、ぽつねんと佇む。

en.html:
Like a lost child giving up on the road, beginning to walk with no destination—

That was how Captain Ootori said it.

Somewhere.
Kahin aur. Somewhere else. No address required yet; first let it not be the place we were going.

Leave this scheme of charging into the Sasagawa Kubo’s seat and killing Shishiku Ootori. A mad scheme—objectively speaking, what else could one call it?
Go elsewhere.

No purpose. If a purpose was compulsory, then escaping the war would do.
Join the crowds already doing that.

No great personage. Just one human being.
Know how small one was. Live within that smallness...

No longer Kanae Ootori. No longer Kageaki Minato.
Neither the pride of noble birth nor the duty of stopping Silver Star.

Naam rehne do. Let the names remain behind. Such heavy names, both of them; perhaps without carrying them, two ordinary people could manage the journey.

Become nobody by choice. Let the world swallow the names.

—Was that what she wanted?
Was that what she had said?

　何処か。
　それはきっと、<ruby>真っ直ぐではない<rt>・・・・・・・・</rt></ruby>何処か……という
意味だろう。

　篠川公方府へ殴り込み、大鳥獅子吼を討つなどと、
馬鹿げた――だろう、客観的にはどう見ても――企て

　目的もなく。強いて決めるなら、戦火を逃れる為に。

　何者でもない、一個の人間として。

　自ら欲して無名の者となり、世に埋没する。

　――そうしたい、と。
　大鳥大尉は、言ったのだろうか。

en.text:
All three agreed. The promise was made.◆
All three knew this someday was never coming.

An ordinary promise, good only for the moment in which it was spoken.◆
The world was full of such promises. Made everywhere, then forgotten, never to be remembered again.

Light conversation. That was all.◆

Today I could not bear the weight of it.

Captain Ootori’s flawless smile hurt to look at.
My eyes escaped to the window.

Changing, yet the same: the landscape filled my sight.
And before it, reflected in the glass—

A shape.
A man.
